utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Cross-examination by Mr. Karadzic: [Continued}

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Franken. Mr. Franken, I would like to move to the critical time period as soon as possible, but briefly I would like to just go over things that preceded that. Did you have your own liaison officer for the Serbian side and separately for the Muslim side, and who was that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had two liaison officers. They served both sides. It was Major Boering and Captain Melchers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was the role of the military observers and how many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number of military observers, and probably you mean the UN observers, was to -- well, to observe, see whether the parties were behaving accordingly, the treaties or the armistice that was there. The numbered varied from two up to three.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. But they didn't do anything for you, did they? I'm thinking of the DutchBat. They didn't do anything for you other than the two of you exchanged information; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not in the organisation of DutchBat. I didn't have any authority over them until the end period. They were posted in the city of Srebrenica. They were not even on our compound. Only in the beginning of July they came to the compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When they took cover before the events; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean by taking cover that they sought for the protection of DutchBat within the compound, then it is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would just like to ask you to look at paragraph 6 of your statement where you talk about the mandate, the mission, and you say that your mission was to deter any hostile action by being present, showing our presence, showing the flag, and then to assist in humanitarian aid and then also the mission was to demilitarise the enclave; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The mission did not provide for combat action on any side, and I think that you also noted with bitterness that after the 9th or the 10th of July UNPROFOR was not impartial any more but had gotten involved in the war.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know whether that was with bitterness, but the conclusion, the note is correct, being a consequence of the fact that we, UNPROFOR, was attacked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you were facing a completely new task to actively defend Srebrenica by all meanings; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the order I got on the 10th, I remember. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the order was issued on what basis? On the basis of what agreement with us?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what -- what the basis was. I only know that I got quite a clear order to defend the city of Srebrenica, which was a completely new, in fact, new situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you, yourself, noted that this was new in relation to the to-date mandate of the United Nations; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It exceeded the existing mandate, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And on the basis of that order you ordered the green task. You issued a green order; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at 1D04743, please, in e-court. 1D04743. Could you please look. Can you tell us what this NL Burum LES is? Is that some sort of a code or what sort of a document is this?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: NL Burum, that is a communication centre in the north of Holland, which was with satellite communications.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And it was your duty in a way to report both to the United Nations and to your own government; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is incorrect. I had to report within the UN line, so directly to the commander of Sector North-east.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. But Burum is a national centre, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's incorrect. It's a NATO centre as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you interpret this document for us, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can, but I think it's loud and clear. I gave orders to Company B to on certain locations defend Srebrenica, and the remark it's a seriously intended green assignment has a history. From origin, we were an elite unit manned for air assault, then we had to do our UN training and we called that blue training, and blue refers to the outfit we had, blue helmet, et cetera. And it was very different from the job, our normal job. So to make very clear to Captain Groen that this was a normal, normal military order, I used that -- that phrase: "This is a green order."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at the next page, please. Our Quick Reaction Forces also foreseen here, and in the order you specify who is supposed to be engaged. We can see that on the second page; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Quick Reaction Forces did already exist. I just put there the Quick Reaction Force of C Company who was based at Potocari under the command of B Company for reinforcement. Your second question, yes, I ordered specifically that Captain Hageman would be the commander of the blocking positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. I was just going to say that this was tendered in the direct case and it's P242.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That was already admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Franken, did you see any difference between close-air support and air attacks, and did you know that this was something that I clarified with His Excellency Mr. Akashi in our discussions?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please move away from the microphone. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, I did it again. There is -- formally air attacks are not a military issue. You can speak of close-air support, which is the operation of one or two planes on a specific target seen by the ground troops. If you speak about air-strikes, because it should be air-strikes, then it is a free hunting area for the air force in a given parameter. So it's not necessary that the ground troops see those targets. And, of course, I'm not aware of your discussion with Mr. Akashi. I was way down isolated in Srebrenica and not getting the information what happened on the higher levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we agree that close-air support is meant as support for UN units which would possibly be exposed to an attack?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as is an air-strike.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, air-strikes, just like General Rose and Mr. Akashi explained, were of a different nature and it was not their objective to defend UN forces in danger but to change the situation on the front, to punish, to alter. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, may we have a cite for this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber knows that already. I cannot keep looking so much. They should know that. We submitted that. My conversations with Akashi and Rose are something that the Chamber knows about. I don't have time to look for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Karadzic, if you don't have time, don't refer to Mr. Akashi or Mr. Rose. You just put your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My case is that we accepted close-air support whenever you were in danger. Both myself and General Mladic said that you were free to respond regardless of who it was that was endangering you, but we were against air-strikes, because in the initial mandate we did not accepted -- accept that nor was that something that was provided. So would you agree that air-strikes are in that sense different from close-air support?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then you are given a, more or less, strategic or political meaning to those two things. I'm a simple soldier. I use air support to defend myself or to neutralise an attacking enemy, and if that has to be done by close-air support, okay. The better means are air-strike, and you can imagine because I described to you what, in fact, the difference is. I would prefer air-strikes. And I'm very sorry, with all respect, what Mr. Akashi and people on that level had with intentions with their air support I do not know of. I can only answer you what, in general, for me as a soldier, close-air support means, air-strike means, and what I prefer being a soldier on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And was it necessary to have visual contact with the Serbian forces, namely, were the forward air controllers required to see the positions of the Serbian forces in order to be of use?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not necessary, because we know the -- the air-borne forward air control as well. What happens then, yeah, well, I'll have to explain shortly the procedure. [Microphone not activated] come in, pick up contact with the forward air controller. He gives information, location and kind of target. Then if it's not in his line of sight, he gives the control over to an air-borne forward air controller who then leads the plane to that target. I hope that's a clear answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And your forward air controllers who were guiding in the fire, were they Dutch, and were they under your command and control, or did you have others?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My forward air controls were Dutch, and hopefully -- no. They were under my control, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have other forward air controllers who were not Dutch?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have forward -- forward -- sorry, forward air controllers other than Dutch. I had a party of British soldiers who were able to do forward air controlling, but they were not a forward air-control party. Sorry, I did not deploy them in that task.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And they did not get their tasks from you, did they?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were co-operating and taking part of our patrol scheme. I -- they got orders from me, but from BH command as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, let's just specify the three lines of separation that you mentioned, the Serbian, the Muslim one, and the one of the United Nations. Could you please look at paragraph 11 of your statement where you talk about those three lines. Can you please tell us how far apart were the Serb and the Muslim lines, and in relation to those lines, where was the line of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, well, the -- the amount of -- of metres they were apart differs on all place -- in all places, which means that the worst case was in the north-east. There, the difference between the Serb line and the Muslim line was about 1.600 metres, and in the south there were differences of 100, 150 metres. And in between that or consistent with the Muslim line, there was the UN border and we took that as being the real border.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In north-east from Potocari up both sides could reach the United Nations by sniper fire but they could not target each other with sniper fire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't judge that. What -- I understand your question as follows: In the area north-east of Potocari, both sides, meaning ABiH and the Serbs, could not fire at each other, but they could fire on United Nations location. Is that what you mean? I think that's incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I think that is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What I would like to know is whether 1.600 metres, does that mean that between your forces and each of the other side was 800 metres, which is a good distance for snipers, whereas 1.600 metres is not a good distance for snipers?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those 1.600 metres were the difference between the Serb and the Muslim line, which does not mean that the Muslims were 1.600 metres away from the Serbs over there, because their positions were over their own border as was with the Serbs. And 1.600 metres away, yes, but actually they were closer to each other there when positions were -- for instance, directly north-east, I forgot the name of that mountain, they were about 300 metres from each other, the defensive positions of both parties. But your question was the formal border on the map, and that's what I answered with 1.600. Again, the distances in -- practically the distances between those units were shorter. They both crawled forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I correct then if I say that of looking at your observation post you had Muslim trenches behind your back, and in front of you, you had Serbian trenches and you were in between; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you refer to Quebec and Romeo, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said, did you not, that no one either from Sarajevo, and I believe you think of your own command, did not explain to you the reasons why the areas were not demilitarised and that you were wondering about that, in fact, that the commands were not exerting pressure to complete that part of the mandate as well.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I recall being puzzled about the fact that they did not explain it. It was part of our mission to disarm the area, and at the same time I say that it was an impossible mission, and I described that before why it was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 12, you talk about how the 28th Division had more or less two headquarters. There was one classroom which were adapted to the needs of that, and then there was the other headquarters in the former post office in Srebrenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Well -- and then again you have to explain headquarters differently from what a normal military unit would call headquarters. They were a kind of offices where they came together and spoke or disputed. It doesn't had the views of a normal headquarters. There were no maps on the wall. There were no communications, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at 1D1994, just so that you can look at their document to see if you knew which facilities they were using as staff and command posts. Or, for example --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just -- Ms. West, I'm looking at the first sentence of paragraph 12 and wonder whether it's correct. It says: "The contacts to the Bosnian Serb Army were through the Chief of Staff of the 28th Division, Ramiz."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I suspect that's a mistake, and if I can address that on redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not intervene, Your Excellencies, but nothing escapes you. I did not intervene because I believe Ramiz, too, is of Serbian origin. Did we get the right document? No, that's D1994, or perhaps it's 1D4769.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, do you know that they were using the facility known as Lovac in Stari Grad? That was the command of the 8th Operations Group. They also used the old headquarters of the Territorial Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sir, did you follow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I could follow the script, Your Honour, but I had for a couple of seconds or minutes no sound on my ear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I had to turn up the volume myself, but -- but you followed. There's no need for him to repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I can read the script. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To -- to answer your -- your question, the location Lovac Stari Grad is not known to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the PTT; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: D199 -- 1994, but if it's 1D, it's 4769. This is it. Did you know that this many privately owned houses had been converted into some sort of military facility, and you have confirmed yourself that private houses were largely used for military purposes; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you mean with my confirmation the house with a lot of communications in -- in Pale, and Pale was a village within the enclave in this case, that's correct. And -- well, knowing about the equipment being in the so-called headquarters we knew of, of course we knew they had to have some other place where they really could operate headquarters, but we didn't know where that house or whatever was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could I draw your attention to item 2 where we see a list of private family houses that had been converted into some sort of military facility. Items 2 or 3 refer to family houses; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can read that. I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we see the next page, please. It also shows various containers and houses and barns, cattle sheds, administrative offices of various businesses used for these purposes. Number 5, 283rd Brigade had its headquarters in the offices of an enterprise. Mr. Franken, one of your difficulties in carrying out demilitarisation was, as you said, that people did not reside in barracks but in their homes. Men would go back to their homes and act again as civilians, and you had no authorisation to search private homes. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct in that sense that because we couldn't define any barracks, our conclusion was that they would stay in homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Considering that you are a professional military man and you always served in professional armies, did you notice that both the Serb and the Bosnian Army were so-called popular armies where soldiers lived in their own homes and rotated on the front line very often wearing civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, I -- that's correct. We observed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that they could also have fired from those houses, that weapons were hidden in haystacks and that those haystacks were often set on fire looking for weapons when the conflict was already in full steam?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a possibility, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And under circumstances when the Serbian army is advancing and the civilians had already left, do you agree it is reasonable to suspect that there might be some soldiers still remaining in those houses who could fire at your back and that it is reasonable to search whatever is behind the troops?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I can imagine another 2 million possibilities, and, yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you speak about sabotage groups, you must have noticed the most drastic cases, and my -- Major Nikolic also informed you about the burning down of the Visnjica village and the killing of civilians and the people who were burned alive in those houses. That was in the spring, just before these events.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said before, Major Nikolic only informed me that there had been an action to a Serb village at the north -- north of the enclave, and he didn't give me any details, even not when I asked for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the Milosevic case in 2003, page 29007, as well as in the debriefing about Srebrenica, 0091388, ERN 014291, you said you had had information about the sabotage operation in Visnjica village, and you knew that some people were burned alive in their houses there.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, and I got a report from my OP Mike as well with details, but your question was -- or you said that Major Nikolic informed me about that, and that was my answer. I said Major Nikolic did not give me any details, just said there had been a raid by Bosnian forces in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now see 1D04695. You see this Ramiz Becirevic, whom you knew as Oric's deputy, he talks about weapons and sabotage groups in Srebrenica. Blast through it and then we'll move to the next page. Could we see the next page, please. He talks about all that happened from beginning to end. Could we see the next page now. Look at paragraph 5 from the top, the parachute operation. Can you recall that aid was air-lifted by parachute, and he says they killed each other for it.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall air-lifted aid. I only thing I know and remember is that I believe twice we had reports of helicopters flying in or over. Afterwards, with our food patrols, we tried to establish where they landed and to find out what happened, but that's the only thing I know. And a parachute drop, if it happens by night, you can't observe that. You can't see that. That could be done absolutely silently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we go two pages further. One more, please. In English. That should be page 5 in English. That's it. Look at this passage: [In English] "After we got those two agreements on demilitarisation of Srebrenica, we had to disarm completely." [Interpretation] A bit further down it says: [In English] "We always had to have several troops." [Interpretation] And look in the next paragraph. It says: [In English] "We obtained after the surrender of our weapons to UNPROFOR, we obtained some material and technical equipment in 1994/1995, which was smuggled through the defence lines and the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Corps." [Interpretation] Do you agree that the evening of the 10th you saw Becirevic near Potocari, and that was the last time you saw the soldiers of the 28th Division, because that night or in the morning of the 11th, they left through Potocari. Do you remember seeing Ramiz Becirevic there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see Becirevic. My CO, Karremans, had a meeting with them in the city of Srebrenica. So I did not see soldiers of the 28th Division at that time. When they were gone next day, the 11th, we -- yeah, well, we -- we -- we stated that fact that they were gone. In that phase we were not familiar with the fact that would break out or break through to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you did know that until the evening of the 10th they were fighting the Serbs, but you could see no such fighting any more as of the morning of the 11th.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I could not see that in the morning of the 11th. We heard and got reported battle noise in the area west/north-west of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm a bit confused by the way in which you conduct your cross-examination. You read out certain passage from this document, a third-party statement, and you asked a question which is totally different from what you've read. There's no -- what's the point of reading out all these passages? You do not take it for granted what's written in third-party statements has been admitted to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not going to tender this statement. I only wish to refresh Mr. Franken's memory about what was going on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you didn't ask a question about the passage you read out. That's the -- that was my point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the 28th Division kept on fighting all the way until the night of the 10th, and as of early morning on the 11th, there was no more fighting in Potocari or elsewhere in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I got reports that there was battle noise, so the conclusion was a larger goal, that the 28th Division was still fighting. The morning of the 11th, there were no ABiH troops, as such, in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see 1D04767. Please look at this. On the 27th May, the order is given to raise combat readiness and to prepare for combat, and it is forbidden to leave the area. Also signed by Ramiz Becirevic. Did you notice at that time that the Muslim side is preparing for some sort of action?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the -- I said before, incidents increased in that period, end May, June, so they were alerted, more alert than normally, but further on I could not, yes, wait in that period. There was some digging of trenches in -- in different places, but that's all what I could see as a reaction to the increased tension.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see 1D04729, order for sabotage actions, dated 5 June. 1D04729. Can this previous document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we saw that document yesterday, and it was admitted yesterday as Exhibit D2009.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. There are not enough of us, and it's difficult to keep up. Then this, too, must have been admitted, this order for sabotage actions. Most of these documents are in evidence already then. I won't waste time on them. Can we see 1D04783.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It seems there is no translation, but I will present it to you now. It's a weekly report on the state of morale submitted on the 30th of June just before the July events in Srebrenica. It lists all the things they had done: "On order of the deputy commander, behind enemy lines our sabotage and reconnaissance groups have been infiltrated. On the 23rd of June sabotage and reconnaissance groups of the 282nd and 83rd Light Brigades returned, and on the 22nd, they carried out the successful sabotage operation just below Osmace village, liquidating four enemy soldiers, destroying a van." For the interpreters, it's on the screen. They should use that: "Two AO have been captured." I don't now what this is. "No losses on our side. On the 23rd of June in Koprivna sector, in a place called Bijelo Stijenje, sabotage reconnaissance groups from the 282nd Light Brigade liquidated three aggressor soldiers and captured one anti-aircraft gun or machine-gun, M72. On 26 June, 1995, behind enemy lines in the area of Vlasenica and Han Pijesak, members of the 28th Division reinforced with a sabotage group from the 280th Light Brigade, a reinforced platoon of the 284th Light Brigade, et cetera, carried out successful sabotage actions if the following sectors: 1, Visnjica and enemy line, fortified Bajtama; 2, in Crna Rijeka sector near the monument at the intersection; 3, in Crna Rijeka sector a place called Bojcino Brdo; 4, in a place called Vrani Kamen. In this fighting around 40 Chetniks were liquidated, various weapons seized," et cetera. Do you think the Serb side was obligated to go on suffering this terror from the protected area, to which it was allowing humanitarian aid to pass as well as everything else they received by smuggling or regular channels? Was the Serbian army expected to continue suffering such losses among its troops and civilians alike?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm surprised that you want an answer from my side of that. No. If you are in defensive positions and the opposite side is launching combat patrols with success, then you have to do something about that. For instance, improve your security measures in your forward line, but again, if you're telling this to me to make clear that there were sabotage actions from within the enclave, that's completely clear to me and never denied by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also knew about Visnjica and this activity. May I now show you something from a VRS source about the same event, about the same incident?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be MFI'd Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI 2014, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at 65 ter 16534, please. I believe there is a translation. I'm sorry, then. Can we see page 4. This is the 26th of June, a report sent to the president of the republic and to the commands of various corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Situation in the territory." Line ten: "The enemy intensified sabotage terrorist groups, especially from Zepa and Srebrenica enclaves. The population is now being informed about the infiltration of sabotage terrorist groups behind the lines of the corps. In the sector of the command post of the Main Staff of the VRS between 1430 and 2130, enemy forces carried out an attack involving three infiltrated groups 15 to 20 men strong. There is information about two more groups. In the course of fighting with the enemy, we had one man killed and three wounded from the 65th Protection Regiment as well as four killed and five wounded from the 67th Communications Regiment. The Muslims also reported civilian victims." Is this consistent with what you knew?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because as I told you before, I got very, very little information from UN side. We were very isolated. The intelligence was, to say it plainly in English, bullshit, so I did not know of this. But again, I will not deny that all kinds of combat patrols, as we call them, were sent out of the enclave into Serb -- into the Serb area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be MFI'd, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder whether the translation of this document cannot be found so far. We should have a translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We checked earlier on this one, and I don't think there is one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D2015, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Regarding the freedom of your movement, you were under considerable restrictions, especially in the so-called Bandera Triangle; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not especially. It was, in fact, the only area within the enclave that we did not have freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in the course of four days one group of four UN soldiers were captured in that area?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a group of four, and they were not captured. I was myself commander of a patrol. The first patrol going into the Bandera, we were with about 40 guys blocked at OP Charlie and another group, another patrol of mine, six or eight guys, in the Suceska area blocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm a bit confused, because in the transcript of your testimony in the Milosevic trial on the 13th of November, 2003, on page 29006, you said that about 100 soldiers of DutchBat III were kept as hostages between 27 and 31 January. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm -- yeah, I can't see whether it's true that I stated that on that, but I think the inconsistency could be because I -- in those 40, I did not count the guys who were at OP Alpha and not able to return to Srebrenica but in UN grounds blocked. What I'm talking now is those 40 were soldiers blocked within the area Bandera. So I think that is the inconsistency you will think there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe that you informed your commands. Was the world public informed of this drastic event?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know of any information in the direction of civilian press, et cetera. I did not see any consequences, but, then again, we did not get papers or whatsoever in the enclave due to the restrictions in convoys, so I -- as far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your view, did the Muslim side envoy a privileged position -- or, rather, a more equitable and better position in the world media as compared to the Serb side? Had the Serb side done this? Would you agree that this would have been hitting the headlines throughout the media?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer your question, I should have been able to see what the media reported about Srebrenica in that period. As I told you before, we did not get that information, so I can't answer the question what would have happened when the Serb side did that or what, because I was not aware of the situation in the media in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to show you a document that is 1D04977. Let us see how all of this looks in the plans of the 5th of January, 1995, of the General Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is. I hope that there is a translation of this document, but I'm not sure. This is the 5th of January, 1995. Kakanj is where the General Staff is stationed. And now can we have page 7. This is a directive, a directive to continue offensive combat activity. It's a document of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm going to read it out carefully if we don't have a translation. So this is what was decided: "The 2nd Corps has the following task: To liberate the area of the mountain of Majevica, Banj Brdo, Stolice, Busija, Povrsnica, Medjednik, the village of Brusnice and reach the road between Priboj, Lopare and Celic. In co-ordination with the 3rd Corps, liberate -- or, rather, cut off the Chetnik forces on the road Klokotnica-Sevarlije and Ozren, and with the assistance of other corps to deblockade the free territory of Srebrenica and Zepa and reach the Drina River from Zepa to Zvornik, and to take part in the deblockade of Sarajevo with part of its forces and on the basis of the decision of the General Staff. The forces of Srebrenica and Zepa have the task to link up all of Kamen, Pogledala, Pribojevici, Bucije and Podzeplje, Rudova Brda, Bulinovici, and to take part in the deblockade of the free territories of Srebrenica and Zepa in direct co-ordination with the forces of the 1st Corps and 2nd Corps on the basis of the decision that they receive from the Main Staff or the corps." So, Mr. Franken, lieutenant-colonel, do you agree that this is a basis of all the activities that you could see in the spring of 1995 and that these are ambitions to take all of the Drina River Valley rather than make life easier for the inhabitants of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it's the basis of all those activities but it could have been, and what I see is a very, more or less, a strategic plan to -- to, indeed, attack in the direction of the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of the fact that Srebrenica and Zepa were protected zones, and in view of the agreement on demilitarisation, did they have the right to plan this kind of thing and take the Drina River valley from these enclaves? I'm referring to the area around the Drina River as Podrinje. Is it legitimate if we take into account the agreements reached with the United Nations and the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you said, Mr. Karadzic, lieutenant-colonel. I'm not a lawyer or anything in that way, so you can't -- I don't think you can ask me whether it is legitimate to plan, and they didn't perform it, to plan an attack in what you see at that moment as enemy territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, if we now look at the activities being launched from Zepa and Srebrenica, incursions into Serb territory, the killing of civilians, is that not in line with this, what had been ordered to them from two protected demilitarised zones? And we are allowing humanitarian aid to reach these enclaves, and around them we should not have any trenches, and our forces should not be tied up in that area at all.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It -- as I already stated, it -- it could have been a consequence of that strategic plan, at least it happened, and killing of civilians is never legitimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm concerned about the frequent usage of untranslated document. Please pay more attention to it and heed to our Chamber's previous ruling. We'll mark it for identification for the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D2016, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you to focus your attention to the following -- or, actually, very briefly, in paragraph 18 you said you were not aware of the fact that the Muslims had not surrendered all of their weapons and somewhere else you confirmed that when these conflicts broke out in July, you offered weapons to them but they were not interested because they had better and more modern weapons; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Do you want a remark? Their better, modern weapons, is opinion of me, it's not in the answer of the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But they refused to take the weapons that you had offered to them, their very own weapons that had been stored at the facilities designated for that. They showed no interest; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we briefly have a look at 16414. That's the 65 ter number. I want to rehabilitate myself in view of the missing translations. This document has been translated. Do you remember that just before New Year's Eve, towards the end of 1994, we signed a cease-fire that was mediated by President Carter, and you were supposed to be there for that cease-fire that was supposed to go on for four months, the well known Carter cease-fire? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that existed when I arrived in the -- in the enclave, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see, only five days after that, the General Staff of the Muslim army passed the directive that we saw a few moments ago about the continuation of offensive activities; isn't that right? That was the 5th of January, 1995.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this document. The Serb army was fully aware of the intentions of the enemy, and it says here in the first sentence: "Having monitored the situation and in assessment of the intentions and capacities of the Muslim forces, I believe that they will not respect the signed cease-fire and cessation of hostilities for four months but will begin in early March their announced spring offensive and will, as part of it, attempt to link up the Zepa and Srebrenica enclaves and then direct their forces towards Kladanj, Olovo, and Tuzla," and so on and so forth. Signature Deputy Commander Colonel-General Manojlo Milovanovic. So do you agree that our army was monitoring the situation and had correct information and correctly assessed what was to happen?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, based on the document we saw before it looks like a good analysis, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2017, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D4766. Can we take a brief look at that now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You confirmed yesterday that you were aware of the structure of the 28th Division, and in relation to the meeting with Zulfo Tursunovic in the Bandera Triangle, your impression was that you were dealing with an organised army; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only in relation to the meeting with Zulfo but, yes, my impression was that it was a divisional organised army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please cast a glance at this. Already in July 1993 there was a structure that stayed on, although later on they were called brigades, the 280th, the 281st, and so on. Are you familiar with this structure of their unit?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Familiar as far as the brigades are concerned. The -- the lower structure and battalions and where they were exactly based was not known to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you see that considerable forces are deployed in villages and could that perhaps be the reason why international visitors who were visiting only the inner city did not see the full strength and structure of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just for the record, I do not remember any international visitors in the period I was there, but it was our problem as well that there were no normal barracks, et cetera, so the contours of a structure were very difficult to -- to -- to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I missed anyone, Doctors Without Borders, the UNHCR, even your own soldiers. Since there was this kind of dispersion in villages, it was hard for you to view their strength without a proper intelligence service; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first, we did not have a proper intelligence service, which is correct. Secondly, well, the problem is that if there is an army and they don't have barracks and they don't all wear uniforms, they're very difficult to recognise as being an army, and if there is a battalion-like unit but scattered over three or four villages and, in fact, housing in the houses present, it's almost impossible for -- it was impossible for us to recognise that as being a battalion or a military unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is something that we call a people's army. Were you aware of Tito's doctrine concerning an armed people, namely that in case of war, each and every individual, no matter where he may be, without any kind of directive or special order, should get a weapon and fight?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, had you been familiar with that, you probably would have seen that all of this was in keeping with that doctrine. Could I please ask you now to focus on the convoys. In paragraph 24, the second part, you say: [In English] [As read] "There were items which the VRS categorically denied. Ammunition, anything that had to do with the weapons system -- systems, spare parts or testing devices, spare parts for vehicles, et cetera, communication radios. Once the list was approved by the VRS, Dutch trucks starting from the areas of Tuzla or Sarajevo would transport the supplies to the enclave. We would inform -- be informed that a convoy had been approved and was scheduled by fax from my logistics base ...," and so on. [Interpretation] Did you understand why the Army of Republika Srpska was placing an embargo on the items that you mentioned in paragraph 24? Would you place an embargo if you had your adversaries in a protected area?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not place an embargo, because -- I thought we discussed that yesterday, but then you stated that the Army of Republika Srpska had no interest in weakening DutchBat. In fact, doing that just by not allowing convoys, and, again, if I saw the role of a UN unit, like obviously, you said yesterday, the Serbs did, then I especially can't understand why there were denials of convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you noted that five or six APCs belonging to the UN were missing from Zepa? It's either the Muslim side that had stolen them or that somebody had sold them.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noted that two APCs -- sorry. You are referring to a UN report from the battalion in Zepa, and I don't remember exactly the number that they reported then. With the number of two, I'm referring to a report of one of my OPs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you see yesterday that a blockade was being planned, your soldiers were supposed to be disarmed, equipment was supposed to be taken. That is what Naser Oric recommended to his deputy.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do believe you that I saw it yesterday, but I do not recollect, but I can imagine that measures like that were taken into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you in the danger of having the Muslim side impose a blockade on you and take your equipment away?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. They could have done that for one OP crew or something, but they wouldn't manage to disarm in that way the complete unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the previous document please be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to this document. It's a 1993 document. The witness could not confirm the locations of the battalions, which is not surprising since it is almost two years earlier than his arrival. I don't think this is the witness for which this should come through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But he confirmed about the brigades.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: He did confirm the number of brigades, but I think the crux of the questioning here were the locations of it, because the Defence went on to say if these soldiers or units were in different little villages, then you wouldn't have known about it. Since he can't confirm these villages from two years earlier, I don't think that this document, if we were to admit it as to his credibility, could then be found against this witness, because it's just -- it's too far in advance of him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond? First of all, the witness confirmed that this kind of structure with different names existed when he arrived as well, and he also confirmed the popular people's character of that army dispersed in houses and villages, which prevented foreigners from observing the strength and structure of the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Witness confirmed the existence of brigade and the manner in which the -- the units were scattered around the villages. On that basis, we have a basis to admit this document. We will admit it as Exhibit D2018. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more document before the break. 1D0473. 1D04773. Maybe that's part of this, but no, I don't think so. This is a separate document. Yes, that's the document. We also have a translation. While we're waiting -- ah, yes, you can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this. This is the state security, the Muslim state security from Tuzla. This is an intercept of a conversation between General Milovanovic and General Nikolai. Some interpreter of his called Svetlana interpreted it and the date is the 8th of July, 1995. The seventh line from the bottom says: "Hello. I'm going to check what this is all about. I am not aware of the problem that the general is referring to. However, the Muslim forces during the course of the day attacked that part of the front line facing us." And then further on: "What I wish to say to the general is that the Muslims over the past few days have been using six APCs of UNPROFOR in the area of Srebrenica." And then: "Your commander in Srebrenica probably knows that and we have located these APCs precisely in the area between Zepa and Srebrenica." And then it says: "I would kindly ask you that you caution your forces to remove all the Muslim's heavy weaponry, especially APCs, or to --" I cannot see the rest. It says "exactly," so probably it's to tell us exactly, and so on and so forth. So do you see on the 8th of July, according to General Milovanovic's information that he conveyed to General Nikolai, the Muslim side had six APCs in the area between Zepa and Srebrenica where the fighting had started; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see as they reported six APCs between -- in the area between the enclave of Srebrenica and Zepa. That is a possibility, but then again, we did not know of them because we did not have any observation possibilities in that area. So it is possible that the ABiH had in that area six APCs, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we mark it for identification? Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D2019, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We're take a break for half an hour, and after which you have a bit less than almost an hour to conclude your cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic. We'll resume at five past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that that's a pity for the Trial Chamber as well, because the witness is very well aware of things that were going on there, and I think that we should avail ourselves of this opportunity, his kindness to shed more light on everything that was happening there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We do not have the luxury of wasting time, reading out all the unnecessary passages from the document. Please heed the advice from Mr. Robinson on how to conduct your cross-examination in the remainder of your cross-examination time. We will resume at five past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just one brief note, the document we looked at before the break, 1D04773, the intercept, I just wanted to note for the record that it's the Prosecution's position that this is not Milovanovic but it's actually Tolimir. The defendant noted it was Milovanovic twice. It doesn't bear on this witness's testimony but I just wanted to make sure the Chamber knew our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did the accused say it was Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: At transcript 2930 he said Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very possible. I apologise for the lack of precision, but Milovanovic did speak often when Mladic was absent, but there can be no harm in being specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D4775, please. We do have a translation. We should be able to see the English version as well. While we're waiting, I just want to introduce the document. This is also the Muslim state security from Tuzla, an intercept of a conversation between General Janvier and General Mladic of the 10th of July. Do we have this translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think we have translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It looks like that. I apologise also. Well, I will introduce it, put it in context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the 7th of July, General Mladic and General Janvier are speaking, and Mladic can be heard better. He's reporting to General Janvier that the Muslims over the last few days, on several occasions, came out of the zone and inflicted losses on the civilian population, burned the village of Vrbica, killed six or seven boys in Lucica, and all of this jeopardised especially the fact that they took equipment from UNPROFOR, especially because they killed some Serbian citizens on the road and inflicted losses on the troops and the civilians. Does this correspond to your knowledge, this information that Mladic is conveying to Janvier?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know of that discussion between those two generals, of course. What I am wondering about in what area is it that this became out of the zone and I don't know exactly the location of Vrbica. Is that in the area of Srebrenica or in another area?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He corrected himself, not Vrbica but Visnjica and Banja Lucica, not Banja Luka but Banja Lucica. Mladic corrected himself. It's all in the environs. He is saying that they would come out of the Srebrenica zone and did this, committed these killings, and you knew about that. You knew about this Visnjica; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I already confirmed that, that it was reported by my OP Mike and a complaint of Major Nikolic of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document. Can we admit it as marked for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D2020, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that you stated that the Bosnian Serb army did not kill a single member of the Dutch Battalion or inflict casualties on the DutchBat, especially not in the enclave, and you said this in the transcript in the Milosevic case; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have stated, yes, we had some light injuries due to Serb fire, but we did not have a lethal kill by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Soldier Rensen was a casualty inflicted by the Muslim side; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Speaking about Serbian army fire, is it correct that you noticed that their objective was to immobilise the movement of the DutchBat or, rather, to immobilise both your forces and the Muslim forces and prevent them from putting up a resistance and not to destroy them; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the context, but did notice that they preferably tried to outmanoeuvre my OPs and then neutralise them after they surrounded them. That is correct. But in the case of the defence of Srebrenica, that objective was not very clear because we came under direct fire. And, of course, by direct fire you can immobilise a unit. That's correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said this in the Tolimir case on the 30th of June, 2010, on page 3339, 3345, also, do you recall confirming that you did not receive information that Serbs had fired at the refugee column and that in your opinion they did have the ways and means of inflicting considerable losses on the column, but they did not resort to that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the last part of your question, they did have the means and -- and -- for inflicting considerable losses. The first part wonders me because to my recollection now I got reports that the refugee column from Srebrenica to Potocari was fired upon by mortars and artillery, and then again the random shelling of Srebrenica is reported and stated by me and not consistent with this, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Some of your soldiers here and an observer of the United Nations, a military observer, stated that they were surprised by the low casualty number. You're talking about 114 wounded. Did you state in transcript -- in the transcript in the Tolimir case on page 3324, on the 30th of June, 2010, as well as in the Popovic case, on the 16th of October, on page 2480 and 81, and there are more references, thus that the Army of Republika Srpska wanted to -- had the Army of Republika Srpska wanted to kill everyone in the column, they could have done that.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said in the Popovic case that civilians, refugees, had set out for Potocari partially on their own initiative and that you agreed, in the same case on page 2610, that you would have definitely been informed had the column itself been bombed, and then again you say: [In English] "They wanted to kill all those people. They had the means to do that."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that there is the same question you said. Yes, if they had wished to kill them all, they could have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In paragraph 60, you are talking about the 11th of July, how the civilian population was moving en masse towards your base. Did you receive information about the Muslim authorities issuing two orders? One of them was for the able-bodied men to go on a forced march towards Tuzla, and for the civilians to go to Potocari and that the civilians in Potocari went there in the desire to be transferred to Muslim territory?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not -- I did not get any information about Muslim orders concerning these things. In fact, as I stated before, they were out of sight on the 11th of July, and I learned through the Bosnian Serb army that they had performed a breakthrough to the Tuzla area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With your permission, may I summarise your explanations, thus: Karremans saw the army of the 28th Division last time on the 10th in the evening. On the 11th in the morning, they were already on their way to Tuzla. On the 11th in the morning, the civilians set off on their own initiative towards Potocari, towards your base. By 11.00 in the morning the town was completely empty, and on the 11th in the afternoon, the Serbian army entered an empty Srebrenica. Was this how it was?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not completely. On the "elf" in the morning they were already on their way to Tuzla. I did not know that on that the very moment. They were not in Srebrenica any more, that is correct. At 11.00 the town was not empty. There were some Muslims still there. Whether that were remaining parts of the 28th Division or what else I know not of, and my blocking positions were still -- at 11.00, DutchBat was still in Srebrenica. On the 11th, we withdrew and the Serbs then entered a completely empty Srebrenica after they tried to enter it on the evening of the -- of the 10th, an attack I described before which we opened fire upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the time that the refugees spent in your base, you estimate that there were about 10 or 11 persons whom you buried, who had died of exhaustion, dehydration. We saw in other cases that there was diabetes, and so on. Were these the people who were buried behind the base?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have to make some difference. I know of there were 11 or 13 persons who were -- who were -- who died within the compound, which we buried on our terrain, in our compound. How many casualties there were outside of our compound, I got some skirmish, not confirmed reports that there were a number of them as well, but again those people we didn't get a hold of and we did not bury them. The number of 10, 11 are official graves made by -- by DutchBat. And, of course I do not know of the existence of diabetes and other diseases within those 35 refugees well. Statistically we've seen on 35.000 people there has to be some people who had to have diabetes, yes, of course, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Lieutenant-Colonel, sir, let's look at these numbers and see if we're sure of them. Do you know that at the time when the enclave held the largest number of people there were some 37.000 persons there, but according to their document, they had reported as 45.000 being there in order to get more aid? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the reason was. They reported 45.000 and 37.000 was a rough estimation made by us just by observation. We didn't count or anything like that. It was just a rough guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: According to their document, they said: "We report 45.000, but please keep that confidential so this does not come out." And they did that in order to get more aid. We do have that document admitted. But at the peak of the overcrowdedness, we know that there were 37.000 people there. Do you agree that more people left the enclave than entered the enclave? The population did not enter the enclave but was going towards Tuzla, and that in 1995 there were fewer than 37.000 people there. The only groups that entered were sabotage groups.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, that's what you say. Again, we estimated the number of civilians in -- in direct surroundings of our compound in the end phase on 37.000, and I don't have an idea how many there were when we came in January 1995. All those numbers as UN is concerned were estimations of the -- the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that there is information also from the Muslim side and from the Serb side, and I believe also from the international community, that 13- to 15.000 set off to reach Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That are the same numbers that I heard of, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then that would make over 50.000 people in Srebrenica. However, it's our estimate that there were slightly more than 30- or 32.000 there. Do you agree in the estimates if 13- to 15.000 were going towards Tuzla then that these estimates were just approximate? They were not precise.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, last questions there was always -- we spoke of estimates of numbers of people, so an estimate is never precise. If you state that, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to dwell on the question of evacuation. Did you know that on the 9th of July, Osman Suljic was trying to find a way for his government to address the Serbs in writing through the United Nations in order to permit the evacuation of the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that Mr. Akashi referred to these consultations with the Muslim government in his letter to Annan on the 11th of July, 1995, where he said based on consultations with the Muslim government we were advised to ask the Serbs for permission for the evacuation of the Serbian population.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take it you mean the evacuation of the Muslim population, but, no, I was not aware of these communications. Again, we never got any communications from that level as info to the DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We do have that footage. Do you know that Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans, at his first meeting with Mladic, said: I am here with the task of asking you to allow the evacuation of the civilian population from Srebrenica? And I think that he even mentioned General Nikolai, that he had received this assignment from General Nikolai.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possible. I personally did not know of that assignment, and I was not present at that meeting, so I had a debrief, but not a literally text that was spoken over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know that Mladic refused to talk about it with the request of returning again late that evening, around 10.30 that evening, with civilian representatives of the Muslim community, with representatives of the Muslims so that the Muslims could state what it is that they want?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know about a refusal. As far as I remember, the debrief of that second meeting was that from the Serb side Mladic proposed the evacuation of the people to be executed by BSA or like that, but that's all what I remember. Again, I wasn't present, and I got a short -- sorry, a short debrief, and I can't judge whether that was complete or enough extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's where the problem lies now. From what we could see and also based on the footage of their meeting indicates that Karremans came with the task of asking for evacuation from Mladic and that Mladic did not say yes or no until the second meeting, first seeking that the Muslims themselves state what it is that they wanted. Had we had time, we could see the footage but I think all the parties are already familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is a waste of time. This witness has already indicated he's not at the meetings. Everything the defendant just said is a statement. There's no question there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but, Excellencies, the witness repeated what is stated in his amalgamated statement, and that is that the idea of the evacuation came from Mladic and that he suggested that this be Kladanj, but here we understood that this was not so. I understand that Mr. Franken was not present at the meeting, and I'm just asking him to re-examine his recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We heard his answer, and even if you do not agree with him, just move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 72 of the amalgamated statement, he says -- Mr. Franken, can you look at that paragraph, please, paragraph 72.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at it, please: [In English] "I heard of the evacuation first the night before. We knew that something would happen in that direction, because I recollect on the second meeting there was already talk about this event, more or less, and that I got the details when Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans came back from the third meeting."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is consistent with what I said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then the next sentence is: [In English] "He told me that it was agreed upon that the Bosnian Serb army would perform what was called the evacuation of the population."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where did you get the idea that Mladic sought the evacuation and that he set the destination, that he had asked for the evacuation at the first meeting and set the destination? Since you were not present, somebody must have misinformed you; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it was misinformation, but I can only recollect what Colonel Karremans told me, and, as I stated in my amalgamated statement and before here, I recollect that there was discussion about that evacuation after or during the second meeting, and it is the meeting on the evening of the 11th and that to my information Mladic came with the proposition about that evacuation. I recollect that there was a theoretical choice for the Muslims to stay or to go, and, again, after that third meeting, I had a very short brief about, well, exactly what is in my amalgamated statement, details. Perhaps for your information I know that the evening of the 11th, that it proves that I am correct in my recollection, the order came from UN by General Nikolai that the battalion had to perform with own means that evacuation of the population, which was not very realistic, but I explained that to General Nikolai.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West, did Lieutenant-Colonel Franken say in his -- in 92 ter statement that the evacuation was proposed by Mladic? Or, Mr. Franken, do you remember that, having said that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In my amalgamated statement, I said, I quote, he told me that it was agreed upon that the Bosnian Serb army would perform what was called the evacuation of the population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It was agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you say that it was proposed by Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my statement I did not, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I just show one document, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know, Mr. Franken, that Mr. Karremans, I believe, or somebody authorised by him, called the defence ministry of the Netherlands and said that an evacuation is being suggested and that after deliberation the minister of defence of the Netherlands said, Yes, go ahead, assist with the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that Colonel Karremans had contact with the defence ministry of the Netherlands. The exact contents of that communication I do not know of. He did all the outer contacts in that phase. I know that at a point I was ordered to assist with the evacuation and that information came through me from Colonel Karremans. The chance that somebody else had contact authorised by Colonel Karremans from within DutchBat and then contact the Ministry of Defence is zero, because the only one that would have been authorised would have been me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that in the Krstic case, on the 17 of October, 19 -- sorry, 2006, page 2582, you said you did not refuse to help during the evacuation because the UN approved Mladic doing this, that the United Nations approved this action by Mladic? Is this the wording you used in that case?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be that the wording is like that, but it is correct. First you -- as a soldier you do not refuse any order, but again, it was UN approved - that was my information at that time - that the BSA did perform that evacuation with its own means. Adjisun [phoen] they told me that ICRC would control the whole evacuation. It was not written. It was verbal, and as usual, an order from Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall that Mladic did not have buses prepared? Instead, he asked for the buses from Karremans, who said he didn't have them either, but he would help provide the fuel, and by 16 July you did provide fuel to the VRS for these purposes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he asked Karremans for the buses, it must have been on the evening of the 11th. So that indicates that there was already on the evening of the 11th discussion about the evacuation. If he asked Karremans for buses, I can believe that he said he didn't have them because that was a fact. I'm surprised by the wish to provide fuel because we didn't have any, and the fuel I gave to the VRS was on the 16th or the 17th, specially brought in by UN, and I was ordered to compensate for the use of fuel the BSA had due to the evacuation. So I was ordered by the UN to give them fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is correct, thank you, but you did not attend that meeting where it was agreed. Do we then agree that the first buses arrived sometime around noon on the 12th from various sites?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether they came from various sites, yeah, obviously, but remarkably was that Colonel Karremans came back from his third briefing and in his -- sorry, third meeting. In his briefing, he told me that it was arranged that there would be evacuation, and the very moment he said that those buses appeared, or five minutes later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 12th; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you do not deny that the Muslim side already in the evening of the 11th had communicated their intentions and their wish to leave.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Communicated to whom, to me?
