utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before Karremans, they asked Mladic to be evacuated to Kladanj or towards Kladanj. If we had time, we would show this footage, but it is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether they asked or whether the destination of Kladanj was ordered I do not know of. The only thing I know is that there was a -- has been a question to the representatives of the Muslim population whether they wanted to leave or not and then the answer was: Yes, we want to leave. And whether that happened during that second meeting on the evening of the 11th or shortly before that, sorry, I can't recollect that, but I know the question was posed to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I should like to show you one short video-clip, my statement given to the Serbian television at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, thought this might be a good time. Can we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now view this interview that I gave at the time referring to the civilian refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. To be clear, we'll put that document we discussed in private session under seal. Do you have a 65 ter number for that video-clip, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 40582. It begins with 16:45 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it also part of trial video?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So it's D4201.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Journalist: The Serb side guarantees safety to everyone in the refugee camp in Potocari and all the Muslim fighters who hand in their weapons and surrender. What is the latest situation, President? "Karadzic: You are right in saying that Srebrenica is top news. It should be a complete example of the superiority of both the Serb weapons and the Serb army and at the same time an example of Serb generosity. Namely, the UN, if they don't have the possibility of protecting the civilians, have the right to have a full insight into what is going on. Our army is enabling the establishing of our civilian authorities there because the Serbs were exiled from Srebrenica at the beginning of the war. Those Serbs are coming back now from the neighbouring villages. There are already existing organs there, elected organs, such as the Municipal Assembly and the Serb organs, and when the affairs settle down an activity of the refugees who want to leave. In fact, the majority, the vast majority of these refugees have declared that they wish to go to Tuzla. It is probable that some of them would declare that they want to go to Abdic, and we are prepared to satisfy their wish considering that each citizen has the right to freely choose where to go, although we think they do not need to. But one thing is certain, this will no longer be a terrorist stronghold. Not a single armed man will be able to remain there except the official authorities and the police, and the citizens of Republika Srpska do not need to leave but most of them want to go to Tuzla and elsewhere."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript was available to the interpreters. I don't know whether you read the subtitles or you read what you heard in the headset. I would like this footage to be admitted until 47:50.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of this Serb position regarding the civilians in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know this interview, of course, and I was not aware of this position. I could only see and observe how the Serbs handled on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you were aware that the option to remain was also available, although you said in practice that option was not very promising.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only promising but purely theoretical. Where did they have to stay? In -- to their opinion, a hostile environment without food, without medical care, without proper housing, et cetera. So theoretically it was an option to the refugees, but in -- practically it was a non-option.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a clarification. Ms. West, is this part of the trial video that we admitted?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where can I find in the index at the end of the transcript updated Srebrenica trial video sources?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President, I'm going to have to look that up. It's going to take me a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or do you have the page number of the hard copy for this part?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And I'm just going to have to look that up as well. Apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm wondering why the Chamber was provided with a separate transcript. Probably it's from the Defence. Then is it because it's not in -- in that book?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I suspect -- I don't know. The answer to the question is I didn't provide that to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We provided it just in case, not knowing how well the OTP is equipped, although we have subtitles on the footage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As indicated by Ms. West, if it is already in the trial video, part that have video, there is no need for you to tender it. Otherwise, I would like to come back to us. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The paragraphs of your statement, 86, 87, and 88, deal with the separation of military-age, able-bodied men, which you did not mention here, but you said in paragraph 86, that in total out of these 30.000, 600 to 700 men approximately were singled out and interrogated to establish whether they were responsible for war crimes. Please look at these three paragraphs. Can you see those three paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I have no hard copy. I see them on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, you observed that, and is it true that you said - let me see where - that it was nothing out of the ordinary and nothing wrong, because there was such a large number of prisoners. You said that in the Blagojevic and Jokic case, 15 September, 2003, page 1501; and in the Tolimir case, that at the end of June 2010, page 3326; in Popovic, 16 October, 2006, page 2497; and also in the Krstic trial, on 4 April, 2000, page 2037, you said you didn't think it was wrong that it was normal to separate those who are suspected of being combatants responsible for war crimes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I stated that and it's true. In those days we learned our own soldiers that there was a big group of population mixed with soldiers, et cetera. You separate the men from them to examine whether they were combatants or not. In that procedure, you don't look for war criminals, but you look for combatants or not. And the military you find are going to be POWs, and then there's -- the procedure as it is is, in those days, a normal procedure. The problem arises when you -- how you treat them, the men, after you've separated them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In any case, you said in Blagojevic, Popovic, and other cases that the separation was carried out properly, but also that it was difficult to distinguish who among them were combatants, because combatants were not wearing uniforms.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You also said, didn't you, that at that time there was no indication anyone would be killed.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning of the -- that is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Could we now see 1D04752, the briefing by your army. You recall that you gave a statement to the Dutch army in the course of this debriefing.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see page 2. We don't have time to see all the paragraphs. End of paragraph one: [In English] "The witness saw that in the last three convoys that left the compound, the men simply walked along with the women, at least as long as they were still in his sight. He also saw two men being briefly separated from the rest but then permitted to rejoin the convoy." [Interpretation] Do you agree that around 250 to 300 men left for Kladanj with their families? They had not been kept behind as combatants.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree on that number because I do not know a number and my observation I gave in the debriefing of the Dutch army is correct. The last convoys as far as I saw them myself and due to reports, the men could join in the buses. That is correct. It's an observation I made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wouldn't agree with the number either, but your soldiers registered at least as many at that time. So the number could only be higher. Look at this: [In English] "The evacuation of refugees was arranged and agreed on paper by General Mladic and General Smith. The battalion had the role of putting the plan into action, and DutchBat had received guidelines in this connection from UNPROFOR." [Interpretation] Is this so? That's what you told your own army?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I told. It is so. It's the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we see the lower part of the page. In relation to the house, the witness -- let me not read this. Could you read it for yourself. Your answer was not fully recorded. You said, "That's not what I told. That was the truth"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. You mean -- yeah. That's not what I was telling it. It is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It must be clear now. Can you see this paragraph? People came in and out of the house. This is also consistent with the truth; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean white house. Yes. People went in and went out, yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There's a reference here to nine bodies found in the meadow near the house, but is it true that nobody saw where and how these people met their death?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they -- we saw how they met because they were all shot and laid there in a row, but there was no UN element present at the very moment that it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you don't know with any degree of certainty whether they got killed there or whether they got killed somewhere else and then were brought there subsequently.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not know. I can only state what I reported, nine bodies in line, all shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have a look at page 3. You say here that Doctors Without Borders had 59 wounded persons that they were taking care of, and you say that you said 239 men who were not separated from their families and while they were within your field of vision. You can see this: [In English] "Medecins sans Frontieres made a list of the names." [Interpretation] and then the next paragraph, starting with the words, [In English] "The witness stated," [Interpretation] et cetera. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Let us not look at this any further then. So you do stand by what this debriefing says; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because it was my statement and according to the truth, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2022, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you have five minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you said that Bosnian Serbs -- or, rather -- well, yes, Bosnian army, were not present when Mr. van Duijn decided on his own initiative to continue with the evacuation? You said that when you testified -- no. No. In the parliamentary inquest on Srebrenica, the 17th of November, 2002, 0308050607 is the page reference. 0607. That's it. You said that Serbs were not present there when van Duijn decided that.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, and as far as I recollect, it was in the morning of the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that between the 12th and the 13th the Serbs were not present at all at your base in Potocari? And that, as a matter of fact, they were late the following morning?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between the 12th and the 13th. You mean overnight? There were some Serb troops, but the unit who was arranging the evacuation left. Whether they were late I do not know, but at the very moment the buses were already there on the morning of the 13th. My Lieutenant van Duijn decided to fill the buses and let them ride because he saw an opportunity to get man in the buses and along the way with those buses. And just for the record, there were never Serbs, just occasionally and individually, there were never Serb troops within my base at Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. 1D4976, can we have a look at that, please. Did you participate in some publication that is entitled: "In the Name of Peace"? Is this your text?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we move on to the next page, please. We don't have enough time to look at everything, but we are going to tender it and then that will do. Please take a look at what you say here: [In English] "The BH army was wiser. They, too, played the blaming game. They had already understood that defence was not possible with 4- or 5.000 men. So the 28th Division made a breakthrough to Tuzla."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "The BH later reported that the breakthrough was successful." [Interpretation] Do you recall that it had been stated by the Muslim side that about 10.000 fighters -- yes, the very top. Do you know that the Muslim side, their state security identified around 10.000 fighters who managed to break through out of the 10- to 15.000 that had set out?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I know that Muslim authorities, and I was back in Holland and reported that the breakthrough to Tuzla was successful. Somewhere in at that report I read that 10.000 men came in. Knowing that at least 15.000, to my knowledge, went away, I was surprised by calling a breakthrough successful. That's why the text is in that chapter, in the book, as it is, was successful, question mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know that from day one various reports said that there were about 3.000 victims during the breakthrough, that there was constant fighting, that there was combat contact between the Serb and Muslim armies and that many, both Serbs and Muslims, got killed?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to have a cite for that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a piece of information. If the witness confirms it, I don't have to look for the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you said that you had, from the day one, various reports, and that is [overlapping speakers] the Prosecution is entitled to ask for that reference.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We have already admitted these papers, Excellency. The Prosecutor should be familiar with the case. We have already admitted this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Without misleading the witness, be precise when you refer to specify reports instead of saying "various reports from day one." Or just put that question yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that the fighting went on even in the Bandera Triangle until the 16th of July? Although the main force broke through fighting still went on even on the 16th in the Bandera Triangle too?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that OP Alpha, which stayed in position up till the 14th, including the 14th, as far as I remember, this report, battle noise, directly eastly from him, and that means in the area Slatina up north. And whether they kept on fighting on the way to Tuzla, I do not know. The only information I had about that breakthrough was later on by Colonel Jankovic who reported to me that they -- due to that breakthrough -- first he said they were performing a breakthrough, and then he said that they had 6.000 men taken prisoner of war. But that is the only information I had in that time about the actions and location of the remains of the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now your last question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, within that last question, can I just exhibit two important intercepts, 30942. That would be the 65 ter number, please. There should be a translation of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We have it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it please be displayed for the witness as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think we need the B/C/S. Yes. Just collapse the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this is an intercept of a conversation. 1240 is the beginning. I can't see the date. The 12th of July. 1240 hundred hours and two interlocutors are saying: [In English] [As read] "Y: We are starting the evacuation of those who want to go towards Kladanj. "X: Okay. "Y: Pass it on ... just let ... provide transportation. "Y: And reinforce with trucks and buses, and a water tank should be sent to give them water and food. This morning we organised it here. We'll give them everything. I talked with them and we'll accept all of the civilians who want to and they can stay. Those who don't want to -- to can choose where they'll go." [Interpretation] So the Muslim side heard these two Serb officials and recorded their conversation. Does this correspond to our claims; namely, that the Muslim civilian population was free to decide whatever it was they wanted?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had that before. I already answered that, that theoretically they had a choice, but I explained it to you that the choice to stay was a theoretic one but not practical. So everybody chose in the end to go out of the enclave. And again, Kladanj was given as a target by Lalic, as far as I know, from the debrief of from Colonel Karremans, and there was no option to anywhere else, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do we agree that this civilian population that was the subject of evacuation, none of them got killed, actually. There were masses of people. None of them fell victim. You saw that, and you received reports. Is it correct that none of them fell victim?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean in the time they were within our, more or less, control, they were victims from suicides, and whether they got killed on the way down to Kladanj or not or mistreated or raped or whatever you can think of, I do not know because the escorts I tried to give were not able to do that job because they were stopped or secluded by the BSA. So I cannot agree on your remark.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But can you agree that you do not have any information or proof of anyone getting killed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's an example of your wasting time. The witness said he doesn't -- he didn't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could this please be admitted, and can we just show the very last document. It's a very short document of the same kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D2023, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 30967, please. Again, we don't need the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, did you know, Mr. Franken, that your soldiers were stopped and mistreated and treated as suspects by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina when they reached Kladanj?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the first party who went in with the first convoy had problems with crossing the confrontation line, and that was Major Boering and Captain Voerman. I know nothing about mistreating -- being mistreated by the ABiH. And if that happened, I'm, in fact, convinced of the fact that I would have been -- reports about that. I know that they were stopped before the -- they could cross the [indiscernible] and had big problems with local Bosnian Serb Army members.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But they were stopped, or rather, not taken in by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; right? When the confrontation line was reached, when there was this sensitive segment that was supposed to be crossed, they were treated as suspects by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they did not want to take them in; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct. Afterwards I heard either was some firing in their direction but that was because a unit, the ABiH unit on that spot was not aware, not informed that they were on the way. And, as far as I know, the [Microphone not activated] the UN unit responsible for that area, then interfered and it went all well. But that is knowledge I got later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please cast a glance at this. This is another intercept. You can see Krstic and Sobot here. They are talking. And Krstic is asking how many buses. I really don't have to read it out myself. You can take a look. And then it says to the tunnel. Krstic says, "Of course." That is where -- [In English] Take care. Nothing must happen to any of them." [Interpretation] Did you see what Krstic says? Is this [In English] proper [No interpretation] [In English] conduct on the part of the commander, [Interpretation] if you will?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If he said nothing will happen to them, it's his solemn wish in this case, and -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Wouldn't you say that that's an order, because he is speaking to his subordinates?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. I didn't know it was a subordinate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, sir, thank you. And please understand that I was not attacking you or Holland or the United Nations in any way. I just wanted the truth to be shown. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West, do you have some re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I do. It's only about five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we continue --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. May this last document be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be marked for identification as D2024. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, we're going to pick up right where we left off, and you were just shown two intercepts, and the first intercepts you were shown was from July 12th at 1240 in the afternoon, and that was the intercept in which Y says: "We'll give them everything. I talked to them, and we'll accept all of the civilians who want to and they can stay. Those who don't want to can choose where they will go." And the question that was posed to you was: Does this correspond to our claims, the Defence claims, that the Muslims were free to decide? Then you were shown another intercept that was just put on the record. That was from the same day but at 13.05. It was about 25 minutes later where Krstic said: "Take care. Nothing must happen to any of them." I want to show you the intercept in the middle which is 65 ter number 30953, please. This is the same day, this is ten minutes after the first intercept. It's at 12.50. It's between Mladic and it says -- and another person. The person says: "Go ahead, General. "Mladic: Have these buses and trucks left? "They have. "Mladic: When? "Ten minutes ago. "Mladic: Good, excellent. Continue to monitor the situation. Don't let small groups of them sneak in. They have all capitulated and surrendered and we'll evacuate them all, those who want to and those who don't want to. "I understand, General." Sir, my question for you is: Is this consistent with what you saw on the 12th and the 13th that everybody was evacuated, those who wanted to and those who didn't want to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as I stated before, yes, that is consistent with my own observations.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Today at page 36 of the transcript, Mr. Karadzic put a long question to you and he indicated that I want -- that he wanted to summarise your explanation and then he put a number of statements to you. And you -- you responded to about all of them, but there's one statement I want to go back to, and he said, his affirmation to you was, in the morning, and this is the morning of the 11th, they, meaning the civilians -- excuse me. In the morning of the 11th, the civilians set off on their own initiative towards Potocari, and I'll ask you this: Based on your observations in the months leading up to this and in the days leading up to this, do you agree that those civilians set off to Potocari on their own initiative?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the -- I missed that. The movement of the population from Srebrenica to Potocari was initiated by our B Company because there was a massive panic within the city due to the shelling. They overrun the compound of B Company in an extent that they were not able to do their military job any more, so B Company contacted me and said that he was guiding them in the direction of Potocari and asked permission for that which I gave. It was, in fact, and does not -- I do not mean that disrespectful but we tried to guide an absolutely stampeding crowd of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I -- just one more quick question. In your amalgamated statement at paragraph 12, it says: "The contacts to the Bosnian Serb army were through the Chief of Staff of the 28th Division, Ramiz." Should this actually be a Bosnian Muslim Army?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That should be the ABiH, the Bosnian Muslim army. It would be a good thing that when the co-ordination of that group between those two parties wouldn't have to had this conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Mr. President, I have no further questions, and I do have the information for the video that the defendant showed. So the video is D4201. The video that was shown, the Karadzic interview, there are three portions of that interview and that's the 9035 video. In regard to the transcript, the transcript is D4202. For the hard copy of the transcript it is page 07047879. That's page 261 in e-court. You asked about the source, that will also be in the book itself, and that page is 8029 and that's page 411 of e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give us the transcript number again?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The transcript number ends in 7879 of the hard copy of the book, which is page 261 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sir, I have just one question. It's your transcript page 35 of today. It's line 2 to 3. Let me go back. I'm sorry, your monitor does not have a scroll-back function. But you said there you got reports that refugee column from Srebrenica to Potocari was fired upon by mortars and artillery. Do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, I did say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What time-frame were you talking about, about firing upon the refugee column?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- they started to move towards Potocari I guess at about 10.30, so the time period I'm talking about is as of 10.30 to 1.00, 1300, but that is an estimation deep out of my recollections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And by stating that refugee column was fired upon; did you mean that refugee column was specifically targeted by Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't prove that, but there was a column on one road, and there were hits of artillery and mortar on that road and in the direct vicinity of that road. There were no military targets or any military movements there except for my B Company being at the tail of that column. So it -- I think it justifies the conclusion that they deliberately shot at the column.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By direct vicinity, what distance do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is indirect fire, sir, so probably they had an observer seeing that column. That could be in parts of the infantry I reported before on my flanks who then gave the information to the firing units and that could have been, as far as I recollect, live mortars. So within 3 or 4 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your paragraph 61 of your amalgamated statement reads like this. After -- after referring to the reports which you just referred to now, you further stated that you: "... ordered base commander Major Otter to find a safe route into the camp because the road in front of our base was in the direct site of Serb artillery and Serb tanks, and I did not want those civilian columns moving up that road because I had reason to believe that they would be fired -- that it would be fired upon." What is the basis for your reason to believe that the refugee column would be fired upon at that time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Experiences in the city of Srebrenica, massive random shelling of the total town, not the edges where perhaps military targets could have been. The shelling of the column on their way down to us and the firing before the mass of the refuse [sic] that they have from that artillery in the area of OP Papa on our base and the facility our base and the warning of General Mladic or through radio that he would not accept refugees to be taken into our camp. Though things together led me to the conclusion that it would be hazardous to let them come in the front gate and have Major Otter look for a different route, a safer route where they weren't cover for that Serb artillery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Lieutenant-Colonel Franken. On behalf of the Chamber and the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tend this, with respect to you, that has not been admitted. That's part of this book. This was a text that was authored by Mr. Franken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2025, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I wanted to thank you for coming to the Tribunal yet again to give it. Now you're free to go. Thank you. If possible I'm going to issue a short oral ruling. I'm asking the court deputy whether it's okay to stay on less than five minutes. Yes, you may leave now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It relates to the next witness. The Chamber is seized of the accused's "Motion to Exclude Evidence of 1993 Srebrenica Crimes" filed on 12th of January, 2012, in which the accused requests that evidence related to crimes committed in Srebrenica in 1993 by Bosnian Serbs be excluded from the amalgamated statement of Mr. Pyers Tucker which the Prosecution will seek to tender pursuant to Rule 92 ter. The Prosecution responded on 16 January, opposing the motion. Having reviewed Tucker's statement and the paragraphs proposed for exclusion, the Chamber agrees with the accused that crimes committed by Bosnian Serbs in 1993 are not charged in the indictment and therefore the accused may not be held criminally responsible for them. However, the Chamber considers that such evidence as contained in Tucker's statement may be admitted as it is relevant to the overarching joint criminal enterprise to remove Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats from Bosnian Serb claimed territory in the BiH from 1991 to 1995, as alleged in the indictment, as well as to the background and preparation of the joint criminal enterprise to eliminate Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica from 11 July 1995 to 1 November 1995. More specifically, it may be relevant to establishing the accused's participation in these two alleged JCE's as well as his mens rea for the commission of crimes, the actus rei of which were committed in July 1995. The accused's motion is therefore denied. Further, the Chamber also wishes to note that the motion was filed less than three working days before the start of Mr. Tucker's testimony when the accused had the statement in his possession for more than two months thus rushing the Prosecution and the Chamber for no good reasons. The Chamber therefore urges the accused in the future and when possible to file such motion sufficiently in advance to allow the Prosecution to respond within the time-frame provided under the Rules. We'll take a break now for an hour and resume at quarter to 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.44 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll be sitting for the remainder of today's hearing pursuant to Rule 15 bis with Judge Lattanzi away due to her official business. Could the witness take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I introduce to you and the Chamber Nathalie Dauphin, who is one of our legal interns from France. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, if you are able to hear me clearly, I wonder if you could please give us your full name for the court record?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: My name is Pyers William Tucker.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Tucker, do you remember giving statements to the office the Prosecutor here at this Tribunal in relation to your service with UNPROFOR in Bosnia and Herzegovina, those statements being in 2002 and 2005?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That is correct. I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you've also testified before this Tribunal on three prior occasions, in the case of Prosecutor v. Stanislav Galic in 2002, Prosecutor v. Naser Oric in 2005, and Prosecution v. Momcilo Perisic in 2009; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in May of this year -- pardon me. In May of 2010, did you sign a further statement for the Office of the Prosecutor consolidating elements of all this previously given evidence we've just referred to?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In preparation to testify here today, were you able to review that statement and the associated documents it referenced?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of that statement with you?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps I could just draw your attention to paragraph number 24 of that statement on page 6 and ask that 65 ter 08556 be called up. Now, Mr. Tucker, this paragraph refers to a letter marked with the number 00412219 which purports to be a letter from General Morillon -- or, pardon me, to General Morillon from a group of Bosnian Muslims dated 24 October 1992, protesting expulsions from Grbavica. Now, the document I've just referred to, 65 ter 08556, should appear on the computer monitor in front of you momentarily. Do you see it now?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this document actually refers to an appeal by -- or is an appeal by citizens from the airport village which is in Sarajevo's district of Dobrinja and has nothing to do with Grbavica; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In light of this, would you like to make a correction or amendment to paragraph 24 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, it read: "This letter is protesting expulsions from the airport settlements."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just to deal with one further correction, perhaps we could jump over to paragraph 167 of your statement where under the heading: "Meetings in Tuzla and Zvornik, 10, 11 March 1993," we see reference in the very last sentence to an incomplete document, one page of an UNMO report entitled: "Special report on situation in Srebrenica area." Do you -- have you found that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And could I just encourage you to pause for a couple of minutes before you answer any questions of mine so that my colleagues in the interpretation booth can do the job they do so well and interpret your answers accurately for Dr. Karadzic and the audience. Could we then, now that we see the paragraph, call up 65 ter 11418. And while we wait for that, Mr. Tucker, since you looked at this document in preparing your statement, we found the missing second page of the document, and 65 ter 11418 is the complete document. I would like you to have a look now at the document that appears on the computer screen, including the missing second page, and just let us know when you've had a chance to review it.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I can see the first page, which was the original page, which -- I can't yet see this -- the second page which was missing. Ah, yes. I can now see what looks like the second page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I wonder if my colleague could please enlarge the second page. Thank you. Now, Mr. Tucker, in respect of this document, your comment was that this note reflected your recollection of events at the time.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, and the second page is consistent with what was going on in Srebrenica at that time when I entered.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, now, having seen the complete document, do you wish to amend or otherwise modify paragraph 167 of your statement in any way?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: No. I believe it's accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any other corrections or clarifications you'd like to make to this 2010 statement?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: There is one omission from paragraph 201, and the penultimate sentence in paragraph 201 says: "However, not a shell has fallen in the town of Srebrenica," and it then ends. That is an incomplete extraction from the original documents, and after "Srebrenica" needs to be inserted "since the arrival of General Morillon." So that the whole sentence is: "However not a shell has fallen in the town of Srebrenica since the arrival of General Morillon."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, does that conclude your corrections or clarifications to your 2010 statement?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if I was to ask you the same questions today which gave rise to the answers in this written evidence, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, they would.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Then with that answer, Your Honour, could I please tender Mr. Tucker's amalgamated statement - it has 65 ter number 90293 - as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4203, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm now read a summary of that written evidence. From October 1992 until March 1993, Pyers Tucker, a British military officer, served with the United Nations as a member of UNPROFOR. He was posted to BH command headquarters as the military assistant to the BH commander at that time, General Philippe Morillon. The witness gives evidence of his observations and experiences during his service in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in particular of events in and around Sarajevo and Srebrenica during his tour. He discusses the incessant shelling, sniping, the cold and hunger endured by the civilian population of Sarajevo. He describes the nonstop shelling of the civilians of that city as terrorism and intimidation. He gives evidence of co-ordinated military operations against areas of Sarajevo and repeated bombardment of the city which could only have been done with the approval of the chain of command of Bosnian Serb forces around Sarajevo. In March 1992, Mr. Tucker travelled with General Morillon to the eastern enclaves --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, that's March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My apologies. Locations including Konjevic Polje and Srebrenica at a time when Bosnian Serb military operations were underway against those Muslim-held areas, progressively squeezing the enclaves and forcing civilians to flee to safety as villages fell one after another to Bosnian Serb control. The impression generated among the civilian population, Mr. Tucker said, was of a relentless unstoppable momentum that could only end with the death of everyone in the enclave. The witness recounts the desperate humanitarian situation faced by thousands of refugees who had crowded into Srebrenica for safety from approaching Serb forces. He gives evidence of the shelling of columns of refugees as they made their way to safety; the shelling of UN forces as they handed out aid to villagers in Konjevic Polje; the shelling of a humanitarian air-lift as it tried to evacuate wounded from Srebrenica; the shelling by Bosnian Serb forces. The witness also speaks of General Morillon's appeal from Srebrenica to the Serbian people, saying that he had come there in the interests of peace. When Morillon left Srebrenica, the situation there for the civilian position exacerbated. The witness accompanied General Morillon during meetings with Dr. Karadzic, General Mladic, and the other political and military leaders of the warring factions, as well as the republics of Serbia and Croatia. Mr. Tucker kept notes of these meetings and based on those drafted reports for his commander for UNPROFOR headquarters and others as necessary. He discusses repeated issues raised by General Morillon with the Bosnian Serb leadership, including the problem of freedom of movement for UN forces and humanitarian aid convoys. Mr. Tucker describes repeated deliberate obstruction on the part of the Bosnian Serbs of the flow of aid to the enclaves. And that concludes the summary.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I do have some questions for you, Mr. Tucker, and I'll try and ask those by referring you to paragraphs of your written evidence, the statement we discussed earlier. First, I'd like to ask you about your observations of the shelling of Sarajevo, and do that in reference to paragraphs 23 and 91 of your statement. In paragraph 23, you describe two types of incoming fire from the Serb forces surrounding Sarajevo, one being concentrated fire, while the other was single shells landing around the city to no military purpose. And yet in paragraph 91, you also refer to something you described as punitive shelling. Could you explain what you mean by "punitive shelling"?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: By "punitive shelling," what I mean is that you would have an infantry attack from the residency forces inside Sarajevo attacking outwards towards Serb-held territory. Generally, the -- these infantry attacks initially made quite good progress because the Bosnian Serb forces did not have as many infantry as the Presidency forces. The Bosnian Serbs would then use their heavy weapons in order to repulse the attack and once the -- they could then bring reserve infantry around in order to push the attacking infantry back to the original position on the front line and then after that they would use artillery during this time. Then after that they would generally shell -- the area of the -- of the city from which the infantry attack had come, and the interpretation was that that was to punish the area from which the attack had come.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Does this then have any relationship to the two types of fire you describe in paragraph 23?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yeah. The -- it would be of the first kind that I described, in other words, concentrated fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And then if we could move forward in time in your statement to the part that appears under the heading 31 October 1992, attack on Sarajevo. There in paragraph 37, you referred to what you described as a co-ordinated military attack launched by the Bosnian Serb army from the north and south of the centre of Sarajevo with the apparent objective of cutting the city into an eastern and western half, and I wonder if you could tell us what -- on what basis you assessed this to be the apparent or the objective of the operation.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The first thing to say is that was the last occasion during the time that I was in Bosnia that the Bosnian Serbs carried out a major attack against Sarajevo that had not been precipitated by a previous attack outwards by the -- by the Presidency forces. Now, how did I know that that attack had taken place? Firstly that I was in Sarajevo at the time and could hear the -- the intense shelling and machine-gun fire and small-arms fire both coming from the -- the north and from the south. In other words, coming from two directions like a pincer movement. Secondly is that that evening, and obviously we wanted to find out what was going on, we had reports on a regular basis from the headquarter Sector Sarajevo at that night from the UNMOs about what they had observed, and the fact that they attacked at the narrowest section of the [Microphone not activated] you could cut Sarajevo in half seemed to indicate that that was likely the objective of the attacks.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like now to move on to a document not included among those referenced in your written evidence and ask that 65 ter 21921 be called up. It's a combat report from Major Vinko Pandurevic, commander of the Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade, dated 15 February 1993, to the Drina Corps command. Perhaps we could collapse the Serbian version if Dr. Karadzic has no objection. Thank you. Now, Mr. Tucker, you had occasion to see this document towards the end of last year in preparation for your testimony at this Tribunal; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to go over to page 2 of the translation of this document, if we could, paragraph 8, which reports that enemy forces in the sectors of Cerska, Konjevic Polje, and Srebrenica have been encircled, among other things. Now, Mr. Tucker, I wonder if you see any relationship between this, in particular, and the operations referred to in this document and the operation you saw mapped out in Major Pandurevic 's office some two weeks later which you mentioned in paragraph 155 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: This paragraph 8 where it refers to the enemy forces in the sector of Cerska, Konjevic Polje, and Srebrenica being encircled corresponds to the beginning situation of the map that was depicted on the map that I saw in Major Pandurevic's office in the beginning of March. Secondly is that the reference to heavy offensive operations from the directions of Teocak, Kalesija, and Tuzla, I'm aware that those -- there were attacks being carried out by the Presidency forces. Teocak I'm not familiar with but Kalesija and Tuzla I am, and I know that there were reports through United Nations reporting that there were offensive operations not at that time but a little bit later, towards late February from those areas towards the enclave in an attempt to relieve pressure on the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we tender this document please, Your Honours, as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4204, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tucker, further in your statement you discuss your stay in Konjevic Polje and at Srebrenica, and I'd like to know if during those periods in the area you had occasion to speak with the local population?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke with the local population in -- or people from the local population in both Konjevic Polje and in Srebrenica, and it was usually through the interpretation of Sergeant-Major Mihajlov, who is General Morillon's body-guard, and sometimes through UNHCR interpretation who were with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In the course of those conversations, did you learn where those people had come from?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. That was usually the first question we asked them, where they had come from.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what did you learn then from their answers?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: They -- the majority of them all came from a number of locations from which they had been ethnically cleansed. The analogy that I make is like a broom sweeping dust in front of it, and there was some refugees who I encountered in Konjevic Polje and in Srebrenica who had been displaced four, five, six times, and had been displaced back in May and then they'd fled for a month and then attacks had come and they'd be displaced again and some had been displaced. And that was the majority because the actual population of Cerska itself was pretty small and Konjevic Polje is just a tiny -- tiny little village. So the vast majority of the refugees had all been displaced multiple times.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps we could move on to another military document, 65 ter 14350, a combat order from 14 March 1993, from Milenko Zivanovic, commander of the Drina Corps. And again, please, if we could -- if there's no objection, collapse the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tucker, this is another document you've seen earlier on or later on last year in preparation for your testimony at this Tribunal; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, paragraph 1 of this document notes that following successful attacks by the corps forces the enemy forces suffered heavy losses especially in personnel, in the general areas of Srebrenica, Skelani, Bratunac, Cerska, and Konjevic Polje, and they also lost much of the territory they held before the start of attacks. I wonder if you could tell us whether that -- I'm sorry. I don't know quite what's happened to the document that's on the screen now. If we could go back up to that first paragraph. Thank you. I wonder if you could tell us whether that corresponds with your observations and recollection of the military situation in those areas at that time?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That first paragraph in paragraph 1 reflects the situation on the ground on the 15th of March. In other words, this was shortly after we had been in Konjevic Polje and just after we had arrived in Srebrenica by which time Cerska and Konjevic Polje had been captured by the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, over on the second page of the translation of this document, if we could flip over there to the first full paragraph on page 2. You see reference to the following, that: "Enemy morale is shaken for the following reasons: Loss of important and large areas" --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry I cannot see that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see the very first paragraph on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Ah, yes, at the top, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. This reads: "Enemy morale is shaken for the following reasons: Loss of important and large areas, and the Nova Kasaba-Konjevic Polje-Drinjaca road being squeezed into an ever decreasing area; heavy casualties, the lack of ammunition and food and constant attacks by our forces." And I wonder if this information is consistent with the mapped progressive squeezing of the enclaves, to use your words, in paragraph 155 that you referred to.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, it's an accurate description of what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have this, please, as the next Prosecution exhibit, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4205, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just before leaving this document, Mr. Tucker, I wonder if from your knowledge, based on your presence on the ground, you have any comment you could make in regard to the estimates of Muslim combat power that we -- if we could go back over to page 1 of the document, that we see reported being in the enclave, and that's depicted in the bottom three -- the final three paragraphs on page 1 of the translation.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: These reports do not reflect the whole situation that was pertaining on the ground. While it is possible that the forces inside the enclave had some of these weapons, they would have firstly only had a very small number of them. Secondly and even more to the point, they had virtually no ammunition for them. It is pointless having a weapon if you do not have the ammunition to fire from the weapon. And this paragraph substantially exaggerates the actual combat effectiveness and capability of the forces, the Muslim forces, inside the enclave. What one needs to understand is that the people inside the enclave did not have organised military forces. They were people, civilians and refugees, who had simply been attacked, and they had no organised military forces, no chain of command, no communications equipment, no weapons, nothing. The weapons that they did have they had seized from -- from their enemy, from the Bosnian Serbs. When I was in Konjevic Polje and when I was in Srebrenica, the average number of bullets for an AK-47 that those soldiers or those people, because they weren't soldiers, they were simply civilians who had been forced to take up arms because they had been attacked, the average number of bullets that they actually had for the AK-47 was less than one magazine, and it was exceptional to see a soldier who had two magazines. I saw one of the two referred T55 tanks in Srebrenica, and the tank had perhaps a couple of litres of diesel left in it and about five or six rounds of ammunition. In other words, its utility in battle was virtually zero.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, you talked about the exaggeration. This seems to be exaggeration. Yes, this paragraph substantially exaggerate the actual combat effectiveness. By that you mean that the Drina Corps command is exaggerating the strength of the enemy forces to its subordinate organs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, in your statement, at paragraphs 198 to 200, you reported on General Morillon's meeting with General Milovanovic at the Yellow Bridge on 15 March 1993, and I wonder if we could, in relation to that meeting, call up 65 ter 08052, please. And this is a document of that very same date, 15 March 1993, from General Milovanovic to the VRS Main Staff, Dr. Karadzic, the prime minister of the Republika Srpska, and the Drina Corps. And you saw this document at the end of last year in preparation for your giving evidence, did you not, Mr. Tucker?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is this a report going up from General Milovanovic to Dr. Karadzic of this very same meeting you discuss in your statement?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. It appears to be the same meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could that be the next Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4206, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now let's move on to 65 ter 09132, which is a regular combat report from the Drina Corps command to the Bosnian Serb army Main Staff, dated 17 March 1993. Is this another document you examined in November of last year, Mr. Tucker?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like you to direct your attention to the last sentence of paragraph 8 of this document, which appears at the bottom of this page, which reads: "I have decided to use part of the forces to tighten the encirclement of Srebrenica and thus force the Muslims to surrender, and use the remaining forces to fortify the lines ..." And we can continue over to the next page so you can see the end of that paragraph. Mr. Tucker, does this decision accord with the military operation you saw sketched out on the map in Major Pandurevic's office at the beginning of March that you referred to in paragraph 155?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could that be a further Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4207, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, moving just a little bit forward in your written evidence to events of the next day, 18 March 1993, and paragraph 206 of your statement, you say there that: "During the day we stayed on the front line to try to hold it open while General Morillon went in his jeep to Zvornik to get the convoy." I'd just like to ask you a couple of questions about that sentence. First of all, briefly, who did you mean by "we"?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Myself and the Canadian army -- armoured personnel carrier and the driver of that vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And where on the front line did you stay?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The Yellow Bridge was in no man's land between the -- the Bosnian Serb forces, which were like First World War trenches and bunkers, and the Muslim forces which were further back in a village and up on the high ground. The Yellow Bridge was in the middle of this no man's land and was a half destroyed bridge, and the gap had been filled with rubble so that with an armoured vehicle, a track vehicle, or a four-wheel drive vehicle you could slowly bump your way over, but an ordinary civilian car would not have been able to cross the bridge. I parked the Canadian M113 on the bridge, on top of the rubble, and that's where I stayed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did anything happen while you stayed there?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: When we arrived, General Morillon spoke briefly with the Serbs at the bunker and at the Serb front line, and General Morillon then drove off in a jeep in the direction of Zvornik in order to go and get the humanitarian aid convoy, and he asked me to stay at the front line in order to try and keep the front line open, because one of the usual excuses used by the warring factions for preventing UN or humanitarian convoys to pass was to stay, Oh, there's heavy fighting there and we can't let you go into danger. So he asked me to stay there in order to keep the front line open so that when he returned with the convoy it would be able to pass. As soon as General Morillon drove off out of sight in the direction of Bratunac, a number of Bosnian Serb tanks and armoured personnel carriers drove out of woods behind the bunker and came out onto the road and drove up through the Yellow Bridge in order to try and attack towards Srebrenica. However, my Canadian armoured personnel carrier was blocking the bridge and it was difficult for a tank to try and drive past. I stood in front of the tank, the leading tank, and gesticulated at the tank to stop and not to go any further. The tanks backed up one behind the other because I was standing in front of the leading one, and then eventually the tanks reversed back behind the Serb front lines and drove into hold-down positions to the left and to the right of the Yellow Bridge. I then went into the bunker and remonstrated with the Bosnian Serb colonel who was the commander at that location. He shouted and screamed at me, and grabbed a Kalashnikov off -- one of his soldiers cocked it, rammed it into my stomach and screamed at me. He then called for the captain of the tank platoon to come into the bunker, and he then screamed and shouted at the tank platoon captain, and eventually they -- they went away. I went back to the armoured personnel carrier, and over the next six hours or so I shuttled back and forth from the armoured personnel carrier to the bunker through the open, whilst a fire fight was going on between the Bosnian Serbs in front of me and the Muslims behind me, and each time I would go to the Serb colonel and say, You should stop firing over there from A to B, and he would say, I will order my men to stop firing there if the Muslims stop firing somewhere else. I would then go back to the armoured personnel carrier, get onto the radio to speak with the UN people who were back in Srebrenica and ask them to speak with the Muslims in Srebrenica to ask them to stop attacking somewhere else. Then I would get a message back from them that they would stop attacking if the Serbs stopped attacking somewhere else yet again, and I went back and forth and back and forth. And the shooting and the fighting got worse, it got less, it got worse. A bit later the tanks tried again to come through and I again stood in front of them and blocked them and told them to go back and they shouldn't go into -- they shouldn't cross the bridge, they shouldn't attack Srebrenica, and then things quieted down and then 20 minutes later the -- suddenly the Serb colonel got into a jeep and drove off rapidly towards Bratunac and then around the corner came General Morillon with the UN convoy.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Tucker. If we could move forward to another document, military document, 65 ter 9006, a combat report from the Drina Corps command to the Bosnian Serb army Main Staff, dated 20 March 1993. And this, Mr. Tucker, is another document you reviewed at the end of last year; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, among other things, paragraph 3 of this document, which is on the second page of the translation you see, records the progress of an UNPROFOR convoy with between 500 to 1.000 women and children to the Zuti Most, which is Yellow Bridge, and eventually to Zvornik. And I wonder, Mr. Tucker, is this the same convoy described at paragraph 212 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And this accords then -- or does this accord with your recollection of the situation at the time?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could that be a further Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4208, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, could you please have a look at paragraph 245 of your statement on the subject of convoys. And 245 appears under the heading: "Meeting with Mladic, Gvero and Buha in Belgrade, 26 March 1993." That paragraph reports four points agreed on as a result of a meeting. The final point listed as being: "A convoy of up to 20 trucks caring aid was to go from Zvornik to Srebrenica on 27 March to deliver and evacuate wounded, women and children on the return journey." Pardon me: "To deliver aid and to evacuate wounded, women and children on the return journey. No men of military age." Do you see that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you aware of whether this evacuation ultimately took place?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I am aware it took place because I was actually in Belgrade at the time, but I saw on television what happens, that the evacuation did take place but that there was a disaster in the loading of the trucks in Srebrenica because the refugees panicked and tried to crowd onto the truck and shots were fired, and, if I remember rightly, there were even a couple of people who were killed by being crushed in the trucks and it was a -- it was reported on television and in the international media and I saw it on television while I was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, finally, I'd like to call up 65 ter 01216, please. This document, Mr. Tucker, is United Nations Security Council Resolution 819, dated 16 April 1993. Now, if we could go over to the next page in this document. Now, point 1 of this document: "Demands that all parties and others concerned treated Srebrenica and its surroundings as a safe area which should be free from armed attack -- from any armed attack or any other hostile act." And if we could scroll down, please, in the document. And at point 5, this Resolution: "Reaffirms that any taking or acquisition of territory by the threat or use of force, including through the practice of 'ethnic cleansing' is unlawful and unacceptable." Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you able to put this document, perhaps, into the context of the events in Srebrenica that we've been discussion and you've described in your written evidence?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. What happened is that when General Morillon and his team, which included me, arrived in Srebrenica on the 11th, 12th of March and found the situation that was so terrible inside Srebrenica, General Morillon then proclaimed from inside Srebrenica that he would declare Srebrenica as a protected area, and this Security Council Resolution is the follow-up of the implementation of General Morillon's demands that Srebrenica be regarded as a protected area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could that be the next Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P4209, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Your Honours, that would conclude my examination-in-chief of Mr. Tucker. And with that, if I may, I'd like to move the associated exhibits referred to in his amalgamated statement into evidence as well, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, I have three questions. The document we saw at the outset of Mr. Tucker's evidence, it's a letter to General Morillon, 65 ter 8556. Can you upload it? Do we have a more legible one? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Unfortunately not, Your Honour. I did look, because it's often the case, but I wasn't able so far to locate a more legible one. Indeed, if I can find one I'll advise my colleague Mr. Reid and it will be uploaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Next question relates to 65 ter 21651, Mr. Tucker's diary. Are you tendering that in its entirety or just page 50, which was referred to by the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, only page 50 referred to by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Finally 65 ter 21986, which was referred to his statement in paragraph 39. I don't think the witness has made any comment about that document. If you are minded to tender that, I wish you to -- I would like you to deal with it with Mr. Tucker now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour, and I'll withdraw my request to tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then all the remaining associate exhibits, other than those that have already been admitted, will be admitted into evidence and be given a number in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tucker, your evidence in previous trials has been admitted, as you heard, in the form of amalgamated statements, and you'll now be asked further by Mr. Radovan Karadzic in his cross-examination. Although we only have 20 minutes, I would like you to start your cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellencies. I should like to remind us all of what we already know, namely that this statement numbers more than 300 paragraphs. I am saying this in view of the time that has been given me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Tucker. May I ask you to shed some light on your mandate, that is, the mandate of UN forces in Sarajevo, and your duties and responsibility that you discuss beginning with paragraph 13. What was the main task, the main mission, of UNPROFOR in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The main mission of UNPROFOR in Bosnia was to facilitate the provision of humanitarian aid to those in need.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall that the presence of UN forces in Bosnia required our consent, and we gave it?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: This is correct. As the Security Council Resolutions under which UNPROFOR was deployed into Bosnia was operating was under Chapter VI of the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The initial mandate based on which we accepted foreign armed presence on our territory never included interference into armed operations; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Strictly speaking you are correct, but if the UN forces were attacked, they had the right to defend themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We agree on that point. You were allowed to defend yourselves. Do you know that General Mladic stated more than once that the UN force is free to respond with fire if they were fired at by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. I've heard General Mladic make such statements through interpreters a couple of times early on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Within that right of the UN force to defend itself, does the right imply also air-strikes or air support, and do you know that we accepted that without any objection?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: While I was in Bosnia, there was never any talk of air-strikes, and so I'm not in a position here to confirm or deny that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Then I won't continue with that line of questioning. I didn't actually mean air-strikes to be precise. I meant close-air support, which differs from air-strikes from what I was able to understand in my negotiations with the UN.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean [Microphone not activated]. When I was in Bosnia in 1992 and 1993, there was never any talk. I never heard any talk of air-strikes or close-air support or any actions from the air. The only actions in the air that came about while I was in Bosnia was the air drops which were started in February 1993 in the areas of the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you then understand why Serb officers were angry when you went out to face Serb tanks and impeded them in their action?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: No, I do not. The Serb tanks were intending aggressive action and were, to my understanding, not adhering to agreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which agreement are you thinking of?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The multiple cease-fires which had been agreed and the multiple occasions when we were told that we had permission to proceed in a particular way, in a particular -- particular direction on multiple occasions during the time I was in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You talk about this in paragraph 14, not about the incident but about the Serbian position. Actually, paragraph 60 - isn't that right? - how you perceived the Serbian position to be the recognition of the Republika Srpska, then a simultaneous cease-fire or truce throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina as opposed to temporary local cease-fires which were proposed by the Bosniak side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: It is correct, but it is not the whole story. The Bosnian Serbs had attacked at the beginning of the Bosnian conflict in April and May and had, through force of arms, seized large territories.
